q: Ammonium hydrogen phosphate, (NH4)2HPO4, is a common fertilizer. How many hydrogen atoms are in one formula unit?
y: Correct: Two ammonium groups give 2 × 4 = 8 H, and the hydrogen phosphate ion adds 1 more: 8 + 1 = 9.
This counts the ammonium H only once (4 + 1). The subscript 2 after the parentheses doubles everything inside.
This counts the ammonium hydrogens but misses the H in HPO<sub>4</sub>.
This multiplies the H in HPO<sub>4</sub> by 2 as well. The 2 belongs only to the parentheses around NH<sub>4</sub>.
h: Hydrogen appears in two places in this formula.
w: Ammonium: 2 × 4 = 8 H. Hydrogen phosphate: 1 H. Total 9 H atoms (with 2 N, 1 P and 4 O).

q: How many atoms in total are in one formula unit of Mg3(PO4)2?
y: Correct: Mg: 3. P: 1 × 2 = 2. O: 4 × 2 = 8. Total 3 + 2 + 8 = 13.
This counts the phosphate only once (3 + 1 + 4). The subscript 2 after the parentheses doubles P and O.
This doubles the P but not the O. The subscript outside the parentheses multiplies every atom inside.
3 is only the number of Mg atoms (or of different elements). Count every atom, including those inside the parentheses.
h: Multiply everything inside the parentheses by the subscript after them.
w: Mg 3, P 2, O 8: 13 atoms in one formula unit.

q: How many oxygen atoms are shown in 3 CO2 (three carbon dioxide molecules)?
y: Correct: Each CO<sub>2</sub> has 2 O atoms, and the coefficient 3 means three molecules: 3 × 2 = 6.
This is the oxygen count for one molecule.
This adds the coefficient and the subscript (3 + 2) instead of multiplying.
This counts the molecules (or the carbon atoms), not the oxygen atoms.
h: A coefficient multiplies every atom in the formula after it.

q: Air is about 78% uncombined nitrogen. Which formula represents nitrogen as it exists in air?
y: Correct: Nitrogen is one of the seven diatomic elements, so uncombined nitrogen is N<sub>2</sub> molecules.
A single N atom is not how nitrogen exists in air; it is diatomic.
This is the nitride ion, found only in ionic compounds.
2N means two separate atoms. In nitrogen gas the two atoms are bonded together, shown with a subscript 2.
h: Is nitrogen on the list of seven diatomic elements?
w: Uncombined nitrogen is N2: H2, N2, O2, F2, Cl2, Br2 and I2 are diatomic.

q: Which of these compounds is ionic?
y: Correct: The formula starts with ammonium, NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, so it is made of ammonium ions and carbonate ions: ionic.
C and O are both nonmetals, and there is no ammonium ion: molecular.
This starts with H and is dissolved in water: an acid (carbonic acid).
C and H are both nonmetals: molecular (methane).
h: A formula that starts with a metal, or with one special cation, is ionic.
w: (NH4)2CO3 contains NH4+ and CO32− ions, so it is ionic even though it has no metal.

q: Which compound below is molecular?
y: Correct: P and Cl are both nonmetals, so they share electrons in molecules: phosphorus trichloride.
Al is a metal, so AlCl<sub>3</sub> is made of Al<sup>3+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> ions: ionic.
NH<sub>4</sub>Cl starts with the ammonium ion, so it is ionic.
Zn is a metal, so ZnCl<sub>2</sub> is ionic.
h: Which first element is to the right of the staircase line?
w: Only PCl3 is made of nonmetals alone with no ammonium ion, so it is molecular.

q: Potassium hydroxide, KOH, is used to make soap. How is it classified?
c: Ionic, because its formula starts with a metal
An acid, because it contains H
Molecular, because O and H are nonmetals
An acid, because it contains the OH group
y: Correct: K is a group 1 metal, so KOH is made of K<sup>+</sup> ions and hydroxide ions, OH<sup>−</sup>.
An acid's formula starts with H. Here the H is part of the hydroxide ion after a metal.
O and H are bonded together as the hydroxide ion, which pairs with the K<sup>+</sup> ion.
A formula ending in OH after a metal is a hydroxide. Hydroxides are not acids.
h: Look at the first symbol in the formula.
w: K is a metal, so KOH is ionic: potassium hydroxide, K+ and OH−.

q: What is the formula of the ionic compound formed by strontium and phosphorus?
y: Correct: Sr<sup>2+</sup> and P<sup>3−</sup>: swap-drop gives Sr<sub>3</sub>P<sub>2</sub>. Check: 3(2+) + 2(3−) = 0.
Each charge number goes to the other ion. Check: 2(2+) + 3(3−) is not zero.
One Sr<sup>2+</sup> and one P<sup>3−</sup> leave a 1− charge.
The subscripts are right, but the cation comes first in an ionic formula.
h: Strontium is in group 2; phosphorus is in group 15.

q: What is the formula of aluminum sulfide?
y: Correct: Al<sup>3+</sup> and S<sup>2−</sup>: swap-drop gives Al<sub>2</sub>S<sub>3</sub>. Check: 2(3+) + 3(2−) = 0.
This leaves each charge on its own ion. Check: 3(3+) + 2(2−) = 5+.
One Al<sup>3+</sup> and one S<sup>2−</sup> leave a 1+ charge.
This is aluminum sulfate. Sulfide (-ide) is the single S<sup>2−</sup> ion.
h: Check the ending: -ide means a single-atom anion.

q: What is the formula of the compound formed by tin(IV) ions and oxide ions?
y: Correct: Sn<sup>4+</sup> and O<sup>2−</sup>: swap-drop gives Sn<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>, which reduces to SnO<sub>2</sub>.
Swap-drop gives this, but 2 : 4 must be reduced to 1 : 2.
One Sn<sup>4+</sup> and one O<sup>2−</sup> leave a 2+ charge. That ratio is tin(II) oxide.
The Roman numeral IV is a charge, not a subscript. Four tin ions and one oxide do not balance.
h: The Roman numeral gives the tin ion's charge. Remember the last step of swap-drop.

q: Calcium acetate is given to some kidney patients to bind phosphate. What is its formula?
y: Correct: Ca<sup>2+</sup> and C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>3</sub>O<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>: two acetate ions are needed, and two of a polyatomic ion need parentheses.
Without parentheses, the 2 runs into the O subscript and reads as "22 O atoms."
Two Ca<sup>2+</sup> and one acetate give 4+ + 1−; the 2 belongs on acetate.
One Ca<sup>2+</sup> and one 1− acetate leave a 1+ charge.
h: Acetate is 1−. How many are needed to cancel Ca<sup>2+</sup>?

q: What is the charge on the cobalt ion in CoPO4?
y: Correct: One phosphate is 3−, and there is one cobalt ion, so it must be 3+.
No subscript on Co means one cobalt ion, not a 1+ charge. The charge comes from the anion.
The 4 counts oxygen atoms inside the phosphate ion; it is not a charge.
3− is phosphate's charge. Cobalt is the cation, so its charge is positive.
h: What is the charge of phosphate on the green sheet?
w: PO43− = 3− and there is one Co, so Co3+: cobalt(III) phosphate.

q: What is the formula of ammonium dichromate?
y: Correct: NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> and Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup>: two ammonium ions, in parentheses, cancel one dichromate.
One NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> and one 2− dichromate leave a 1− charge.
Without parentheses, the 2 runs into the 4 and reads as "42 H atoms."
This is ammonium chromate. Dichromate is Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup>.
h: Find dichromate on the green sheet, and treat ammonium as one unit.

q: What is the formula of zinc hydroxide?
y: Correct: Zn<sup>2+</sup> and OH<sup>−</sup>: two hydroxides, in parentheses, cancel one Zn<sup>2+</sup>.
Without parentheses, the 2 applies only to H: one O and two H. Two whole OH groups need parentheses.
One Zn<sup>2+</sup> and one OH<sup>−</sup> leave a 1+ charge.
Two Zn<sup>2+</sup> and one OH<sup>−</sup> give 4+ + 1−; the 2 belongs on hydroxide.
h: Zinc is a fixed-charge metal. What is its charge?

q: What is the formula of the phosphate ion?
y: Correct: Phosphate, from the green sheet, is PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>.
Phosphate is 3−; 2− is the charge of hydrogen phosphate, HPO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>.
This has one fewer O, so it is phosphite.
This is phosphide, the -ide ion, with no oxygen.
h: Phosphate is one of the -ate ions to memorize.
w: Phosphate is PO43−, the ion in bone mineral.

q: Dried apricots from the Valley are often treated with sulfur compounds that form the SO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> ion. What is the name of this ion?
y: Correct: Sulfate is SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>; one fewer O with the same charge is the -ite ion.
Sulfate has four O atoms. This ion has three.
Sulfide is S<sup>2−</sup>, with no oxygen.
Sulfur trioxide is the neutral molecule SO<sub>3</sub>. The 2− charge makes this an ion.
h: Compare the number of O atoms with sulfate, SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>.
w: One fewer O than sulfate, same charge: sulfite, SO32−.

q: Chlorate is ClO3−. What is the formula of the perchlorate ion?
y: Correct: Per-...-ate means one more O than the -ate ion, with the same charge.
This has one fewer O than chlorate, so it is chlorite.
This is hypochlorite, two fewer O than chlorate.
Adding an O atom does not change the charge; perchlorate is 1−, like chlorate.
h: What does the prefix per- do to the number of oxygen atoms? Does it change the charge?

q: Some toilet-bowl cleaners contain the hydrogen sulfate (bisulfate) ion. What is its formula?
y: Correct: Sulfate is SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>; one added H<sup>+</sup> makes the charge 1−.
Adding H<sup>+</sup> lowers the negative charge by one: 2− becomes 1−.
This is hydrogen sulfite (bisulfite), built from sulfite.
This is sulfuric acid, a neutral compound with two H.
h: Start from sulfate. What does adding one H<sup>+</sup> do to the charge?

q: What is the name of the ion Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup>?
y: Correct: Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup>, with two Cr atoms, is dichromate, from the green sheet.
Chromate is CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>, with one Cr atom.
Both chromium ions on the green sheet end in -ate.
The per- prefix is not used with chromium in this course; count the Cr atoms instead.
h: Count the chromium atoms.

q: What is the formula of the peroxide ion?
y: Correct: Peroxide, from the green sheet, is two bonded O atoms with a 2− charge.
This is the oxide ion, a single O atom.
This is the neutral oxygen molecule, with no charge.
This is the hydroxide ion.
h: Peroxide has two oxygen atoms.
w: Peroxide is O22−; hydrogen peroxide is H2O2.

q: Zinc oxide, ZnO, is the white ingredient in many diaper creams. Which name follows the naming rules?
y: Correct: Zn is on the fixed-charge list (always 2+), so no Roman numeral; O<sup>2−</sup> is oxide.
Zinc is a fixed-charge metal, so it takes no Roman numeral.
Ionic names never use prefixes.
The anion takes the -ide ending: oxide.
h: Is zinc on the fixed-charge list?
w: zinc oxide: fixed-charge metal, no numeral, no prefixes.

q: What is the name of MgBr<sub>2</sub>?
y: Correct: Mg is group 2 (fixed 2+) and Br<sup>−</sup> is bromide.
Ionic names do not use prefixes.
Magnesium has only one charge, so no Roman numeral.
Bromate is BrO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>; a single Br is bromide.
h: Fixed-charge metal? Single-atom anion?

q: What is the name of PbO?
y: Correct: One O<sup>2−</sup> means the single lead ion is Pb<sup>2+</sup>: lead(II).
Lead forms two ions, so the name must include a Roman numeral.
No subscript on Pb means one lead ion, not a 1+ charge. The charge comes from the oxide.
Lead(IV) oxide is PbO<sub>2</sub>, with two oxide ions.
h: Work out lead's charge from the oxide ion.
w: O2− = 2−, one Pb, so Pb2+: lead(II) oxide (plumbous oxide).

q: Some water-treatment plants add ferric chloride to clump particles together. What is its formula?
y: Correct: Ferric is iron(III), Fe<sup>3+</sup>; three Cl<sup>−</sup> cancel it.
This is ferrous chloride, iron(II). -ic is the higher charge.
The charge 3+ is not a subscript on Fe. Three Fe<sup>3+</sup> and one Cl<sup>−</sup> do not balance.
One Fe<sup>3+</sup> and one Cl<sup>−</sup> leave a 2+ charge.
h: Does -ic mean iron's lower or higher charge?
w: Ferric = Fe3+; with Cl−: FeCl3, iron(III) chloride.

q: Copper fungicides sprayed in Valley orchards often contain Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub>. What is its name?
y: Correct: Two OH<sup>−</sup> give 2−, so the copper ion is Cu<sup>2+</sup>: copper(II).
Copper forms two ions, so the Roman numeral is required.
Ionic names do not use prefixes.
Cuprous is copper(I), the lower charge; this copper ion is 2+, the higher charge.
h: Find copper's charge from the hydroxide ions.

q: What is the formula of copper(II) chloride dihydrate?
y: Correct: Cu<sup>2+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> give CuCl<sub>2</sub>; di- means two water molecules.
Copper(II) is 2+, so it needs two chloride ions.
Dihydrate means 2 H<sub>2</sub>O, so a 2 goes in front of the water.
This puts the Roman numeral in as a subscript on Cu and never reduces; copper(II) chloride is a 1 : 2 compound.
h: Write the ionic formula first, then the dot and the number of waters.

q: Sodium bicarbonate, NaHCO<sub>3</sub>, is given by IV in some emergencies. What is its other accepted name?
y: Correct: HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> is hydrogen carbonate (bicarbonate), and Na is fixed at 1+.
Sodium carbonate is Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>, without the H.
Adding H does not change the -ate ending; the ion still has three O atoms.
Sodium is a fixed-charge metal, so it takes no Roman numeral.
h: Bi- is the older way to say one added hydrogen.
w: HCO3− = hydrogen carbonate: sodium hydrogen carbonate. (Context only; not treatment advice.)

q: What is the name of SiCl<sub>4</sub>?
y: Correct: Si and Cl are nonmetals: one Si (no prefix on the first element) and four Cl = tetrachloride.
Molecular names need a prefix to count the Cl atoms.
Mono- is never used on the first element.
Name the elements in the order they are written in the formula.
h: Two nonmetals: count the atoms with prefixes.

q: Strike-anywhere match heads contain P<sub>4</sub>S<sub>3</sub>. What is its name?
y: Correct: Four P = tetraphosphorus, three S = trisulfide.
Without prefixes, the name does not tell you the formula; P and S form several compounds.
The second element needs the -ide ending.
The element written first in the formula is named first.
h: Prefix + first element, prefix + second element with -ide.

q: Valley dried-fruit packers treat apricots with sulfur dioxide gas to keep their color. What is the formula of sulfur dioxide?
y: Correct: No prefix on sulfur means one S; di- means 2 O.
This is the sulfite ion, which carries a charge. Sulfur dioxide is a neutral molecule.
The di- belongs to oxide, so the 2 goes on O, not on S.
Di- means two oxygen atoms.
h: Which element does the prefix di- belong to?

q: A dental office offers nitrous oxide to anxious patients. What is the formula of nitrous oxide?
y: Correct: Nitrous oxide is the common name of dinitrogen monoxide: two N, one O.
This is nitric oxide (nitrogen monoxide), the gas used in neonatal intensive care.
This is nitrogen dioxide, a brown air pollutant.
This is dinitrogen trioxide, with three O atoms.
h: Its systematic name is dinitrogen monoxide.
w: Nitrous oxide = dinitrogen monoxide = N2O. One subscript changes the compound completely.

q: A student names Na<sub>2</sub>S "disodium sulfide" and CS<sub>2</sub> "carbon sulfide." Which pair of corrected names is right?
y: Correct: Na<sub>2</sub>S is ionic (Na is a metal): no prefixes. CS<sub>2</sub> is molecular: prefixes required.
Sodium is a metal, so Na<sub>2</sub>S is ionic, and ionic names never use prefixes.
CS<sub>2</sub> contains only nonmetals, so it needs a prefix for the two S atoms.
Sodium is a fixed-charge metal, so it never takes a Roman numeral.
h: Classify each compound before naming it.
w: Ionic Na2S: sodium sulfide. Molecular CS2: carbon disulfide.

q: What is the name of BrF<sub>5</sub>?
y: Correct: One Br (no prefix on the first element), five F = pentafluoride.
A molecular name must count the F atoms with a prefix.
Mono- is never used on the first element.
The first element in the formula is named first, and the second gets -ide.
h: Count the atoms of each element.

q: Which name for Cl<sub>2</sub>O follows this book's prefix rules?
y: Correct: 2 Cl = dichlorine; 1 O = monoxide, with the o of mono- dropped before oxide.
Before oxide, the final o of mono- is dropped.
Mono- is used on the second element, so oxide needs mono-.
There are two chlorine atoms, so the first element needs di-.
h: Check both prefixes, and the vowel before oxide.
w: dichlorine monoxide: di- on Cl, mono- on oxide with the vowel dropped.

q: Parietal cells in the stomach produce HCl(aq). What is its name?
y: Correct: Chloride (-ide) in water becomes hydro- + chlor + -ic acid.
That is the name of pure HCl, a gas. The (aq) means it is dissolved in water and takes an acid name.
Chloric acid is HClO<sub>3</sub>, from chlorate. HCl has no oxygen.
Binary acids end in -ic, never -ous.
h: No oxygen in the formula: which kind of acid is it?
w: Chloride → hydrochloric acid. Without water, HCl is hydrogen chloride gas.

q: Nitrogen fertilizers are made from HNO<sub>3</sub>. What is its name?
y: Correct: The anion is nitrate, NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>; -ate becomes -ic.
-ous comes from nitrite, NO<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>, with two O atoms.
Oxyacids never take hydro-.
The -ate ending changes to -ic in the acid name.
h: Name the anion first, then change its ending.

q: What is the formula of hydrobromic acid?
y: Correct: Hydro-...-ic means a binary acid from bromide, Br<sup>−</sup>; one H<sup>+</sup> cancels it, in water.
This is bromic acid, from bromate. Hydro- means no oxygen.
Bromide is only 1−, so the acid needs one H, and there is one Br.
This is hypobromous acid, from hypobromite.
h: What does the prefix hydro- tell you about oxygen?

q: Rhubarb leaves contain oxalic acid. What is its formula?
y: Correct: Oxalate is C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>; two H<sup>+</sup> cancel its 2− charge.
One H<sup>+</sup> cancels only half of oxalate's 2− charge.
This is acetic acid, from acetate.
This is the oxalate ion; the acid is neutral.
h: Oxalate has a 2− charge. How many H<sup>+</sup> are needed?

q: What is the name of HClO<sub>3</sub>?
y: Correct: ClO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> is chlorate; -ate becomes -ic.
-ous comes from chlorite, ClO<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>.
Hydro- is only for acids without oxygen, such as HCl(aq).
HClO<sub>4</sub>, with four O atoms, comes from perchlorate and keeps the per- prefix.
h: Which chlorine oxyanion has three O atoms?

q: Which acid is named with the prefix hydro-?
y: Correct: HF(aq) contains no oxygen: it is a binary acid from fluoride, so it is hydrofluoric acid.
HNO<sub>2</sub> contains oxygen: nitrous acid, no hydro-.
H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> contains oxygen: carbonic acid, no hydro-.
HClO<sub>4</sub> contains oxygen: perchloric acid, no hydro-.
h: Hydro- is used only when the anion is an -ide ion.
w: Only binary acids (no oxygen) take hydro-: HF(aq), hydrofluoric acid.
